messages.author: 4b681bcd9d4d425d
messages.subject: Massive slowdown from setting threads=2 (not 1)?
parts:
I'm running Stan via R, with a single core. (This is just for testing for now.)

I have a model that ran in about an hour with the R command;
stan(file='fit_SIS_Generic.stan', data=data_trial,iter=100, chains=1, seed=194838, refresh=20)

(I am aware that this is too few iterations, etc. Again, this was for testing.)

I changed that slightly, to 
stan(file='fit_SIS_Generic.stan', data=data_trial, iter=100, chains=2, seed=194838, refresh=20),

and the first chain took about 5 times as long, per the updates delivered (the second chain was still running and I killed it after a dozen hours.)

There are other problems with the model, but I was surprised to see that running chains=2, where they run in sequence, not in parallel, should affect the timing - especially given the indetical random seed, which I would think gives the same process and results, though this may not be true when running multiple chains. 

I looked at the manual, and the only thing I could find was that there were differences that could occur in how the model runs due to thread safety for multiple chains.

Is there a different / better explanation?

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Massive slowdown from setting threads=2 (not 1)?
parts:
Back to the original question: David, is your computer swapping? Do you get the same slowdown using CmdStan?

I suspect that the posterior for the Stan program you've written is ill-behaved and that might be causing your problems:
- how reasonable are your results? do they differ run to run? are there divergent iterations? are you hitting the tree depth limit?
- can you try adding stronger priors to see if that will help?
- I would suggest trying to run more warmup iterations. Perhaps the adaptation parameters are not being tuned anywhere reasonably.
- is the model non-identifiable?


Daniel

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Massive slowdown from setting threads=2 (not 1)?
parts:
If you’re running with multiple chains then the seed gets incremented for
each chain to ensure that they don’t all give the same results (i.e. the
RNG will be independent for each chain).  Consequently when running
multiple chains you should not expect the same exact results, and
one chain can easily get stuck in a pathological region if your model
is ill-posed.

On Sep 7, 2015, at 5:46 PM, David Manheim <davidm...@gmail.com> wrote:

There are tons of problems with the model, which I'm trying to address. The version that is displaying this behavior is probably having multiple issues, including identifiability, and divergence - but within any one thread, given the same seed, I would think it shouldn't take different amounts of time depending on whether there was another thread scheduled to run afterwards. That was the reason I thought this was worth bringing up as a potential issue.

On Saturday, September 5, 2015 at 7:53:33 AM UTC-7, Daniel Lee wrote:
Back to the original question: David, is your computer swapping? Do you get the same slowdown using CmdStan?

I suspect that the posterior for the Stan program you've written is ill-behaved and that might be causing your problems:
- how reasonable are your results? do they differ run to run? are there divergent iterations? are you hitting the tree depth limit?
- can you try adding stronger priors to see if that will help?
- I would suggest trying to run more warmup iterations. Perhaps the adaptation parameters are not being tuned anywhere reasonably.
- is the model non-identifiable?


Daniel

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Massive slowdown from setting threads=2 (not 1)?
parts:
It is perhaps possible that the threads are executed out of order, i.e. the second one first. If there are multiple chains and a specified seeds, Stan winds the PRNG forward by some fraction of its period depending on the chain_id. This ensures that you are not using the same random numbers across multiple chains but it would also mean you can get very different behavior across chains.

Ben
